Long document retrieval has been a significant challenge due to its memory and computation requirements, particularly when dealing with lengthy queries. To address this, researchers have been exploring self-attention mechanisms that can condense document information into fixed-size vectors. However, these approaches are highly sensitive to label noise, which is common in large-scale retrieval models. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the label noise robust document ranking (LR-DR) method, which utilizes bag sampling and group-wise loss to resist corruption during long document ranking. We demonstrate the efficacy of LR-DR on the LongCLIR benchmark and show that it outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, even when labels are noisy. Our code is available on GitHub.

This study addresses the challenge of semi-supervised learning on graphs when
severe label scarcity occurs, a scenario that existing methods are ill-equipped
to handle. To this end, we present GPL, an innovative pseudo-labeling approach
that prioritizes the selection of label scarcity and misclassification risks
when choosing pseudo-labeled samples. Specifically, GPL devises an adaptive
selection framework that leverages Pseudo Label Risk and Pseudo Label Scarcity
to iteratively choose pseudo-labeled samples and refine the classifier.
Furthermore, GPL introduces Pseudo Label Importance to mitigate the influence
of noisy pseudo-labeled samples on supervised learning. Comprehensive experiments
on diverse datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed method.

Betatron radiation spectroscopy in a wakefield accelerator can serve as a sensitive tool for diagnosing the dynamics of non-linear strong focusing. This research explores how the distribution of radiation emitted by particles undergoing oscillations within the plasma wake generated by an intense, short plasma wave driver can be analyzed. A simulation examines the potential of using this technique in an upcoming experiment in which a plasma column, 10 meters in length, is employed to accelerate electrons with high energy. The study investigates the influence of electron injection timing relative to the plasma wave on the characteristics of the resulting beam and beam dynamics. By examining beams with low and high emittance and 1 GeV and 100 GeV energy, the analysis reveals the distinct features of the beam's energy distribution resulting from strong focusing. A significant high-energy component in the radiation spectrum, caused by the strong focusing effect, is observed to be present in both pre-accelerated and post-accelerated beams, with the potential to distinguish between them through plasma-based deceleration.

The growing need for privacy protection in data analysis has led to the development of algorithms that balance personal data security and model accuracy. While the research into privacy-preserving data release methods is extensive, its application to widely used machine learning models like decision trees remains underdeveloped. Our study addresses this gap by proposing and validating the accuracy of two fully private decision tree models. The first model, PrivateCART, is a privacy-preserving adaptation of the commonly used classification and regression tree algorithm. The second model, PrivateID3, is an alternative implementation based on the ID3 decision tree method. The models were tested on real-world datasets, with the results demonstrating their ability to produce accurate results while protecting personal data. The study also highlights the difference in outcomes between private and non-private data and offers potential improvements to machine learning models and their performance in privacy-preserving environments.

We focus on the variational inference task of minimizing a R\'enyi divergence between a model and a data distribution under constraints, utilizing a constrained optimization approach. This method transforms the problem into a projection problem onto the convex hull of the base measures, which we solve using Bregman proximal gradient algorithms. These algorithms are analyzed and exhibit a convergence rate of $O(1/n)$, which is further improved to a bounded sequence via demigenerations, yielding $O(1/n^{2/3})$ convergence. This framework is applied to several families of divergences, including $\alpha$-Bregman divergences, and is utilized in variational inference for mean field variational autoencoders and importance sampling.

This generalises the Bayesian methodology developed by Aalen and Duedal (2019) to encompass the more extensive class of probabilistic models identified by Fieller (1954) and Fieller et al. (1958), which includes Chain Event Graphs (CEGs) as developed by Briers (2006). A Bayesian framework is established for CEGs by employing Dirichlet process priors, which facilitates maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation and the derivation of the corresponding posterior distribution. This approach is demonstrated to be effective in addressing real-world problems, including a CEG model for the Danish prison system and another for the German pension system, which directly compares two distinct CEG model specifications.

In a Hilbert space, we develop a damped inertial dynamic with a vanishing
regularisation term that strongly converges to the minimum norm solution of a
closed convex subset's projection. This dynamic is a combination of the
forward-backward framework, Tseng's splitting framework, and Tikhonov
regularisation, with the regularisation term gradually diminishing over time.
We establish a relationship between the forward-backward framework and Tseng's
splitting framework in handling monotone operators and show that the dynamic
strongly converges to the minimum norm solution under the condition that the
regularisation term's rate of decrease is slower than $1/t$. Furthermore, in
our framework, we show that the regularisation term's rate of decrease can be
arbitrarily slow, surpassing the $O(1/t^2)$ rate often seen in the
literature. This research provides a continuous-time counterpart to iteratively
applied forward-backward and Tseng's splitting methods, each using the minimum
norm solution of Tikhonov regularised monotone operator finding and closed
convex subset's projection as their regularisation step.

This study examines the behavior of a mobile robot with a collective approach to navigating its surroundings. By analyzing a pair of coupled agents, we identify two distinct methods for one agent to influence the other, in contrast to traditional wall-following techniques where a single agent adjusts its position based on its two neighboring spots. Our investigation into the first interaction method reveals a range of complex dynamics, including chaotic movement and transition patterns that are affected by the robot's speed. The second method, however, shows a more straightforward, predictable pattern when one robot adjusts its position relative to the other, yet we find that both methods produce the same pattern of transitions when two or more robots are involved. Additionally, we have also looked into the time it takes for the robots to adjust their positions as a way to measure their interaction.

Within the framework of a kinetic energy driven superconducting mechanism, the effect of impurities on the transport properties of cuprate superconductors has been investigated, utilizing the tight-binding model. It has been observed that the coexistence of superconductivity and a pseudogap can be naturally explained, and that varying impurity concentration significantly affects the superconducting transition temperature, peaking at a specific impurity concentration threshold. Additionally, impurities have been found to suppress superconductivity more profoundly than charge carriers, and contrary to previous models, their scattering effects do not follow linear or quadratic trends with respect to the density of charge carriers, but instead display a quadratic relationship, consistent with experimental findings. A comparison with available experimental data on the microwave conductivity of cuprate superconductors has been conducted, and it has been found that the impurity scattering effects are quite significant, accounting for a substantial portion of the conductivity, particularly at low frequencies.

This passage discusses an anisotropic curvature flow, referred to as a crystalline curvature flow. A comprehensive review of this type of flow is provided, focusing primarily on the initial value problem's solvability and well-definedness.

Our proposed method, GrowSpace, utilizes a combination of visual cues and corresponding actions to train, based on visual observations, the sequence of actions required to achieve a desired plant shape. GrowSpace addresses the challenge of learning plant shaping by framing it as a task involving identifying the necessary tools and sequence of movements to achieve a desired shape. This problem is simplified by training through identifying the essential tools rather than the detailed sequence of movements. GrowSpace addresses this challenge through three key components: a network that learns to identify required tools, a tool selector, and a generator that creates a sequence of movements. GrowSpace demonstrates its effectiveness by achieving superior results compared to existing methods, particularly in complex and multi-step plant shaping tasks.

Using the Fefferman-Graham-Schramm theory of conformal welding, we develop an interpretation of the SLE loop as a quantum disk. We then build on this understanding to explore the behavior of SLE loops when viewed through the lens of h-disks with varying moduli. In addition, we build upon this theory by examining the SLE loop's behavior as a h-disk with infinite modulus, effectively transforming into a h-hemisphere. Our investigation also extends to multiple SLE loops, specifically a pair of loops with distinct parameters, as this setup corresponds to a two-punctured quantum disk. We then expand our analysis to the case where the two p-hyperspheres merge into a single, two-punctured h-hemisphere.

The Image Biomarker Standardisation Initiative is a global partnership focused on developing consistent methods for image biomarkers, enabling seamless integration of information across different platforms and applications, including clinical, research, and imaging environments.

We have analyzed the production of $K\Lambda$ and $N\pi$ particles in reactions involving a nucleon, taking into account the contributions of nucleons in high-spin states, a delta resonance, and fundamental baryon interactions. Our calculations have been compared to experimental data from the DA$\Phi$NE-E948 experiment, and we found that the predicted outcomes are in line with the observed results. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that the magnetic dipole moment $L_{M1}$ and electric quadrupole moment $E0$ play a significant role in these interactions.

This research details the process of preparing the MORPH-II dataset, which is split into two groups based on whether the individuals involved in the image have undergone a significant life event. The morphing operation involves exchanging facial features between source and target images to generate intermediate images. By utilizing Python and the OpenCV library, we demonstrate how to process these images for face recognition analysis.

A reduced curvaton spectrum width can cause primordial black holes to form after the curvaton nonlinearly interacts with the inflaton. The resulting formation of PBHs can be attributed to curvaton fluctuations that originate from the interaction between the curvaton and inflaton fields. The study reveals that the primordial black hole mass distribution exhibits a non-Gaussian characteristics due to running curvature perturbations generated by the curvaton-inflaton interaction. The researchers suggest that this phenomenon can be investigated through PBH detection methods such as gravitational waves, gravitational lensing, and gravitational perturbations.

This research introduces a statistical framework that uses observed milestones to map out university curricula. Building on the success of observed learning sequences, our proposed model considers a student's individual characteristics, such as their academic history, to provide a more comprehensive analysis. The model in question is an extension of the Factor Analysis model, which we have adapted to be a discrete version suitable for categorical data. We have derived an efficient algorithm to estimate the model's parameters, using both analytical and stochastic methods, which converge to provide reliable results. The proposed model was tested on actual university curriculum data, which is available in an open database, and our results were compared to a baseline approach. The model was then used to uncover a student's academic trajectory based on their features, which is a crucial step in generating personalized learning recommendations.

This paper addresses the challenge of vehicle platooning, where multiple automated drivers must maintain a cohesive line. To achieve this, we've developed a novel method based on differential games, where each participant aims to achieve a specific goal while considering the actions of others. Our approach is rooted in a Bregman multi-agent optimization framework, where each participant seeks a balance between achieving their objectives and minimizing effort. In the context of platooning, our method ensures that the group maintains a compact formation, yet remains resilient to disruptions. By utilizing Newton's method, we can efficiently obtain the optimal solution, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach through a simulation of ten automated drivers.

This study investigates offline learning methods for logistic regression when dealing with very large datasets that cannot be processed due to communication constraints. To address this challenge, two new approaches are introduced: the first is Communication-Free Logistic Regression (CFLR), an algorithm that avoids all communication by using numerical precision manipulation, allowing it to achieve test accuracy comparable to traditional batch gradient descent while being more efficient in terms of communication. To further increase sample speed, a second approach is presented: Communication-Free Stochastic Gradient Descent (CSGD), which reaches test accuracy comparable to stochastic gradient descent but avoids communication. To demonstrate scalability, CSGRD and CSGD are parallelized across multiple machines, allowing them to complete a training epoch at a rate proportional to the number of processors. To demonstrate the effectiveness of these approaches, they are applied to learn the parameters of the large-scale IMDB dataset, showing comparable test accuracy to their counterparts in terms of computation time, while significantly reducing communication overhead by 2 to 3 orders of magnitude.

The widespread dissemination of misinformation through the internet has become a significant concern, exacerbated by the ease of creating and distributing misleading content. This problem is compounded by the challenges associated with filtering out spammy and fake news, particularly in the case of automatically generated headlines. In an effort to address this issue, we have developed novel features for classifying headlines that were subsequently used in conjunction with the [11], [12], and the recently introduced BERT models. Our proposed approach achieved an accuracy of 92.5% on the dataset.

In this study, we examine a polycrystalline spin-1/2 kagome lattice and compare it to an amorphous network with a similar topological structure to investigate the possibility of a chiral spin liquid in the lattice framework. The researchers used cluster exchange models to analyze a kagome cluster glass and a locally kagome network, respectively. Their analysis shows that the formation of chiral loops is influenced by the ratio of stronger to weaker nearest-neighbor exchange interactions. A specific phase diagram is developed for both models, which reveals that the chiral spin liquid emerges under similar conditions in the two different lattice frameworks.

Future large-scale radio interferometers like the Low Frequency Array and the Square Kilometre Array will greatly enhance our ability to study the universe at lower frequencies. However, these instruments also introduce greater challenges in terms of calibration due to their increased sensitivity and complexity. In this research, we've developed new efficient calibration methods with a linear-logarithmic scaling, making them suitable for large, grid-based interferometric arrays. Our solutions involve leveraging the fast Fourier transform's efficiency to exploit correlations between different signal channels. By identifying and learning the calibration parameters in stages, we've demonstrated the feasibility of these schemes and their potential to significantly reduce computational time. Our results indicate that the proposed methods can effectively handle the calibration needs of large, grid-based interferometers, thereby facilitating real-time data processing.

An essential component of portfolio diversification is risk reduction, which can be effectively achieved by employing a long/short strategy with negatively correlated assets. However, this approach is often complicated by the presence of multiple factors and non-stationary risks. To address these complexities, we utilize a combination of deep learning techniques, specifically the autoencoding conditional GAN model, to generate a set of transformed stock returns that are both statistically similar to the original returns and diversified by the sign. The feasibility of our method is demonstrated through results on several US stocks, which show improved performance in terms of diversification and risk reduction when applied to raw returns, which in turn leads to significant enhancements in portfolio returns and reduced risks.

We have calculated the polarized massless matrix element $A_{gq}(N)$ for
introducing a light quark or antiquark into the flavor scheme, for the first
time for the $O(\alpha_s^3)$ order in the Mellin moment $N_*=N_1+N_2$,
where $N_1$ and $N_2$ are the first and second moments, respectively.
Additionally, the $A_{gq}(N_{*})$ calculation is accompanied by the $O(\alpha_s^3)$
expressions for the polarized structure function matrix elements
$\tilde{A}_{gg}(N)$, $\tilde{A_{qg}}(N)$, and $\tilde{A_{qg}}(N)$.
These calculations are necessary for a future precise determination of the
proton's polarized light-quark and gluon distribution functions.
The $O(\alpha_s^3)$ order is particularly important for the accuracy of
these functions, given the high precision with which gluon distribution is
known.
The results are based on the calculation of the three-loop polarized light quark
or antiquark distribution function $f_{i/g}^{(3)}(x)$, which is provided in
a separate paper.
The findings are presented in a compact form, specifically for $N_*=2$,
$N_*=3$, and

As the primary source of high-energy gamma rays, blazars are extensively studied. 
Recent findings from multiple studies suggest that Fermi-LAT has the capability to 
observe blazar activity, a capability that can be utilized for large-scale
classifications. In this research, a selection of 724 Fermi-LAT blazars was 
assembled using the NED catalog and light curves, then analyzed by comparing
their spectral properties and flux levels. The results indicate that a Bayesian
neural network is able to accurately categorize the selected blazars, 
demonstrating an accuracy of 67.4% for binary classification and 80.3% for
multi-class classification.

Social media has significantly transformed the way people communicate online, diversifying content types and platforms. To effectively utilize social media, content creators must be proficient in digital skills, content creation, accessibility, and platform navigation. This research focuses on social media accessibility, examining current research, barriers, and potential solutions for enhancing social media inclusivity. Our study draws on relevant literature, a social media literacy model, and theoretical frameworks to understand and improve social media accessibility.

In this paper, we define and investigate the concepts of tensor join and independent set for hypergraphs using hypermatrices, and then establish some key properties related to the spectrum of hypergraph join operations. We also provide a construction for non-trivial self-independent hypergraphs.

India has long been involved in space astronomy research, with the 1990s seeing the launch of the 1.2m Ulysses telescope for near-Earth observations and the creation of the Raman Research Institute's 1.3m telescope at the Gwalior Observatory for multi-wavelength studies. However, a large, advanced space-based observatory has been a priority since the early 2000s, with the INSIST mission being a significant space-based spectroscopic and imaging initiative. This mission aims to observe the universe from 400 nm to 2.5 $\mu$m, utilizing 1000 integrated arcseconds of angular resolution and 1000 nm/R of dispersion. With an estimated 1000 hours of observing time, the telescope will focus on four primary areas: cosmology, galaxy evolution, star formation, and exoplanet research.

In clinical trials for Alzheimer's disease, monitoring progression is crucial, and a new method using natural cubic splines has been developed to analyze time-to-event data. This approach, known as the cubic spline method (CSM), offers a more accurate and flexible alternative to traditional methods like the Kaplan-Meier estimator and Cox proportional hazards model. By employing these nonparametric techniques, the CCM and CSM can handle various trial scenarios without making restrictive assumptions, while still providing efficient, robust, and reliable results. Furthermore, the CSM can handle complex data patterns and non-linear effects, unlike the Cox model, which often assumes a constant effect over time. Through comprehensive simulations, the CSM has been shown to outperform the Cox model, particularly in terms of statistical power and accuracy. Additionally, the CSM has been applied to a real-world study of Alzheimer's disease, comparing the efficacy of donepezil and placebo treatments.

A novel computational method has been developed for identifying pathways of system transformation between two equilibrium states. This algorithm optimizes the action functional to determine pathways that are most likely to occur, which are characterized as dominant transition pathways. By employing an action-based approach, researchers can determine a single reaction coordinate that effectively captures system transformation. Utilizing optimization techniques, the algorithm identifies trajectories between these states, which can then be used to construct a global reaction coordinate. This coordinate divides all transition pathways into categories based on their frequency of occurrence. Testing the algorithm on a series of models, including a 2-well and 3-well potential, a protein folding model, and an adsorption-dissociation model, demonstrates its effectiveness in accurately capturing system transformation.

This study focuses on a parabolic version of the complex Monge-Ampere equation and utilizes a PDE-based method akin to the maximum principle to derive the $L^{\infty}$ and $C^{2}$ estimates. We further extend these results to the Hessian equation and incorporate a range of $G$-equation types, including the $\sigma_k$ operator. Building upon the $C^{2}$ estimates, we establish the local $C^{2}$ and $C^{1}$, along with the global $C^{1}$ estimates for the given parabolic Hessian equations. Finally, with the aid of the Arzela-Ascoli theorem and the Isemberg-Semler-Williams theorem, we demonstrate the existence of smooth solutions to the mentioned parabolic Hessian equations.

Building on a 1991 discovery by Sch\"{u}tte, we create new typed lambda-calculi and show they surpass the capabilities of regular functions with recursive structure. Our calculi, based on existing type systems, introduce additional features to achieve this, specifically adding well-bracketing predicates directly to their types. By incorporating these lambda-calculi into dependent type systems, we can enhance their type-checking efficiency.

This concise note establishes a relationship between Ito and Stratonovich integrals when conditional measure flow components are involved in the integrands, with the 'correction' term requiring consideration of Lions-type functional derivatives in this context. It also provides an explicit expression for the L Lions functional derivative when a conditional measure flow is applied to a regular function with compact support.

This paper introduces the concept of a normal structure space for groups, and demonstrates that for any given group, this space is compact and Hausdorff. It also defines a function mapping subgroups to subsets of this space, and shows under specific conditions, these images are compact and Hausdorff. A central hypothesis of this work states that every subgroup of a given group is a closed subset within this space, with significant implications for the study of abstract groups.

This study tackles the cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing issue, where a pre-trained model is used for domain-specific parsing without the need for labeled data in a new domain. Current approaches often rely on pre-trained models and domain-specific parsing, but a key limitation is the lack of direct connections between encoded text and SQL data. To overcome this, we propose an auxiliary task that links text and SQL by finding matching properties in a table, and we also introduce a novel pre-training model that enhances the understanding of cross-domain text and SQL data by leveraging a large volume of labeled data from various domains. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through cross-validation experiments on real-world text-to-SQL datasets, which outperforms current state-of-the-art models significantly.

This study addresses the navigation of a single robot and a group of multiple robots in a multi-robot system to minimize collision risks. A data-driven approach is used to develop a probabilistic navigation model based on observed frequencies of human and robot interactions, which is then integrated into a risk-sensitive model predictive control (MR-SMPC) algorithm. By applying this method, the probability of an unaccepted event involving the single robot is minimized while navigating towards its destination. A real-world test involving a human and multiple robots was conducted to evaluate the proposed MR-SMPC method, which demonstrated its effectiveness in avoiding collisions with humans and robots.

The key to understanding the properties of dark matter lies in examining the mass-to-light ratio of dwarf galaxies within the Milky Way. Our analysis of the Andromeda XXV galaxy, derived from Gaia data, reveals a mass of $1.2^{+0.5}_{-0.4} \times 10^6 M_{\odot}$ and a distance of $57.7^{+1.1}_{-1.0}$ kpc from the Milky Way. Key characteristics include a stellar mass of $2.2^{+0.5}_{-0.2} \times 10^3 M_{\odot}$, a half-light radius of $102^{+10}_{-8}$ pc, and a mass-to-light ratio of $11^{+3}_{-2} M_{\odot}/L_{\odot}$. Our kinematic analysis indicates that Andromeda XXV is a member of the Milky Way's system, and its central dark matter density is significantly lower than that of the Milky Way's Sagittarius Dwarf Galaxy, suggesting a link between dark matter density and initial galaxy mass.

In massive machine-type communications (mMTC), grant-free access plays a vital role, and non-orthogonal access sequences are a key component. However, traditional designs are limited to mMTC applications, with low throughput. This paper presents a novel approach to sequence assignment using a two-stage genetic algorithm (TSGA) for use in mMTC. The proposed method enhances the current solutions by allowing for more effective search spaces and better sequences that minimize the mean square error at the receiver. The effectiveness of TSGA is demonstrated through simulations, which show that it outperforms existing solutions by significantly reducing MSE, yielding up to 100 times improvement.

A few fundamental principles are presented to ensure the reliable integration of numerical models into the research of atmospheric thermodynamics. These guidelines are derived from the consistent application of thermodynamic theory and the accurate representation of physical properties like density and the speed of sound within these models. Several models have been developed for specific applications, such as numerical simulations and radar data interpretation, but they often deviate from general thermodynamic principles due to their limited scope. We examine some of these models, including the commonly used ideal gas law approximation and more sophisticated approaches like the August-Roche-Cirault formula and its updates, highlighting their respective limitations and inaccuracies. We then present improved alternatives that adhere to the principles of thermodynamic consistency and accurately describe the speed of sound in moist air under various conditions, including high pressure and low temperature scenarios.

We introduce algebraic objects, which generalize ordered semirings and ordered semirings, to expand upon them. Using generalized ordered semirings, we define new algebraic structures that include matroids, leading to the establishment of matroid exterior and Clifford algeras. These matroid algebras allow us to compute the Clifford and exterior algeras directly from a matroid, using its closure operation. Research demonstrates that the Clifford algebra is isomorphic to the extended exterior algebra, and both are independent of the specific matroid used for their construction. These findings enable the Clifford and exterior algeras to be used as invariants in matroid analysis. Various properties and identities specific to these new algeras are also explored.

Research has shown that dialogue state tracking models can benefit from the uncertainty inherent in speech recognition models. However, current methods for modeling this uncertainty are limited, often restricted to a limited number of top speech recognition outputs or simplified neural sequence-to-sequence models. These approaches may not fully capture the complexity of speech recognition output uncertainty. In this study, a new method for modeling word uncertainty is proposed, using word confusion networks. Experimental results using the spoken dialogue system for managing restaurant and hotel bookings demonstrate that incorporating word confusion networks into the dialogue state tracking model leads to a significant decrease in error rates, with a 20% relative reduction in output error.
We calculate the number of injective semistable coherent sheaves on a smooth projective curve, with a fixed rank and degree, in terms of the shuffles of integers.

A crucial component in secret sharing and access structure analysis is the concept of universal structures, which can be used to create smaller, complex secret sharing schemes. However, there's a significant challenge in efficiently identifying these universal structures due to their corresponding decision problem being NP-complete. In this study, we provide a detailed characterization of which universal access structures can be implemented in polynomial time using treewidth analysis, thereby making the decision problem more tractable. Additionally, we examine the computational complexity of identifying structures that utilize the smallest possible number of components, which has applications in minimizing the required fields or primes in secret sharing schemes.

We present a method for optimally estimating the amount of entanglement in a mixed state of two qubits, using an optical setup with path encoding. By employing either displacement or phase-gate operations, we can accurately measure the amount of entanglement for various initial states. Notably, our approach also enables accurate identification of when two states are separable by setting a specific threshold. Experimental results show good agreement with our findings and demonstrate a precise threshold value of approximately 0.15, allowing for reliable estimation of entanglement.

The long-lived palm tree modes (PTMs) observed in the ion edge in H-mode plasmas have been studied extensively at the JET tokamak. A thorough analysis of the mode's characteristics, including its spatial and temporal behavior, has been conducted using a combination of experimental data from density fluctuations and simulations from the ZFAB model. This investigation has revealed that PTMs originate from the lower plume region where ion temperature gradient (ITG) turbulence is prevalent. Furthermore, the correlation between PTMs and the location of the gradient transport radius suggests that the primary source of these structures is the 2D turbulence in the lower plume. A combination of the primary source's location and the downstream interaction with the electron transport boundary in the far scrape-off layer (SOL) explains the mode's formation and asymmetry. A combination of the primary source's location and the interaction with the electron boundary in the far SOL also explains the mode's disappearance in helium-free plasmas. A combination of the primary source's location and the interaction with the electron boundary in the far SOL also explains the mode's disappearance when the ratio of helium concentration in the plasma to the electron transport boundary in the far SOL is also considered.

A recently developed class of deep learning models, known as pre-trained models, have been extensively studied in the field of deep learning. Their capacity to learn and adapt to various tasks is highly valued, particularly in the context of continual learning where they are expected to avoid using previously learned information for subsequent tasks. In this study, we investigate the continual learning capabilities of pre-trained models, and specifically the two prominent ones, known as MoJo and RFCNet. Our research reveals that these models are unable to achieve significant performance improvements when using unsupervised review. In fact, they often perform worse than the standard baseline. To address this issue, we propose a basic alternative approach, the "copy baseline", which involves using a model with no prior knowledge and replicating its performance for each new task. Our results show that the proposed method consistently surpasses the pre-trained models, raising questions about the necessity of using pre-trained models in the context of continual learning.

This paper presents an innovative approach to identifying harmful content on social media by integrating multimodal learning with a focus on explaining the results. A new dataset, Contumelia, has been created, consisting of text and image pairs from the Facebook comments section, categorized into hate speech, offensive speech, and appropriate content. A proposed framework for offensive speech detection leverages deep learning techniques to analyze visual and textual components, employing contrastive learning to guide the model. Additionally, the framework employs novel attention mechanisms to interpret the connection between the image and the offensive speech, thereby offering a more nuanced understanding of the phenomenon. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, with a notable improvement in effectiveness. Furthermore, our approach's ability to provide explanations for the detected hate speech is validated through a linguistic analysis of the comments.

We investigate the behavior of large networks of theta neurons by analyzing how different connection patterns affect slow oscillations. By examining the interactions between fast synaptic connections and slow intrinsic oscillations, we establish a model that captures the emergence of theta rhythms in neocortical regions. Our analysis reveals that the statistical properties of neurons, specifically the distribution of degrees, significantly influence the synchronization of neurons. By deriving equations for the evolution of neural phases, we determine the conditions under which neurons synchronize and how the connection pattern affects this process. Our results demonstrate that the typical neuron phase velocity is a key factor in determining the synchronization threshold, and that the synchronization behavior is sensitive to the connection pattern's structure.

Recent years have seen significant interest in Automatic Program Repair (APR) with
several approaches attempting to fix bugs in code automatically.  Despite their
varied success rates, these methods often rely on specific datasets and training
processes, which limits their general applicability.  We introduce Adversarial
Patch Generation (APG), an innovative technique designed to generate program
repair suggestions that aren't influenced by training data.  By using the existing
code structure, APG creates a set of potential fixes without any direct reliance on
training information.  Our approach has shown promising results on multiple
datasets, demonstrating adaptability and the ability to generalize across diverse
programming domains.

This study utilizes a broadened definition of fading channels to develop precise formulas for both the capacity limits and optimal coding strategies of two specific network types: a graph and an interconnected structure with two nodes. The generalized definition encompasses a range of fading channel models, including those based on a graph. Additionally, we have developed a strategy that maximizes the rate at which information can be transmitted over the described interconnected networks under all possible fading conditions. Notably, although our findings are derived for more complex channel models, they also provide insights into the optimal coding strategies for the simpler, original models under consideration.

The flow analysis technique developed in the 1990s has been instrumental in exploring the nuclear equation-of-state up to the present day. A significant limitation of this flow analysis is its applicability to transverse flow measurements in 2-dimensional space. A proposed extension of the flow technique into 3-dimensional analysis is discussed, specifically in the context of the ALICE experiment at the LHC. A comparison of 2-dimensional and 3-dimensional flow measurements reveals that the latter is more sensitive to the equation-of-state, particularly to the stiffness of the equation-of-state. A critical aspect of the flow analysis technique is the identification of the point at which the flow saturates, which is essential for the precise measurement of the nuclear equation-of-state. A proposed novel approach to determining this saturation point is discussed, which leverages the symmetry of the data to reduce statistical uncertainties.

The rapid spread of COVID-19 has been a major concern, with significant impacts on the global economy and life expectancy, as well as causing a large number of fatalities and infections worldwide. Recent advancements in deep learning have shown promising results in the medical field, particularly in the analysis of CT images for COVID-19 detection. However, traditional methods of using CT images for diagnosis can be impractical due to their time-consuming and expensive nature. As a more efficient alternative, using clinical text data has gained attention, as it is readily available and can be efficiently processed. This research focuses on developing a robust clinical text analysis model that can accurately detect COVID-19 patients while safeguarding their sensitive medical information through the application of adversarial training techniques, which also helps in removing irrelevant data and enhancing the robustness of the model.

A Graph Neural Network (GNN) based machine learning approach is proposed to address wireless communication system optimization issues. This decentralized inference method involves a single-round computation, eliminating the need for machine learning training data transmission. By utilizing graph neural networks, the proposed scheme effectively models various wireless communication problems and demonstrates performance parity with traditional deep neural network (DNN) solutions, all within the constraints of a single round of computation.

This paper examines homicide rates in Brazil's Goias state from 2002 to 2014, 
focusing on how rates varied by age and sex. Our analysis reveals distinct 
patterns in homicide rates among different age and sex groups, indicating that 
most homicides involved males under the age of 30. Three clusters of cities 
were identified: cities with very high, very low, and average homicide rates. 
Low inter-county variation was observed among groups A and B, whereas group C 
showed significant variation. Our findings suggest that our approach can aid in 
identifying areas requiring targeted crime prevention strategies.

The stochastic gradient descent (SGD) algorithm is a key method for training machine learning models. However, its performance can be limited by the presence of noise in data. Research has shown that a modified variant of SGD, which adjusts step-sizes dynamically, is more effective for a certain type of noise in data. In this study, a noise-adaptive variant of SGD is developed that can adjust its step-sizes automatically without needing to estimate the noise level in data. The algorithm's ability to adapt to different problems and data is also demonstrated. Furthermore, a variant of this algorithm is tailored for use in accelerated settings. Theoretical analyses confirm that the algorithm's results are comparable to those of state-of-the-art methods and are supported by practical experiments.

Axions are a prime candidate for dark matter, and their existence can be
investigated by analyzing solar core fluctuations using BabyIAXO, a tabletop
variant of the IAXO concept. By applying Bayes' theorem, we can infer the likelihood of axions based on the detection of their conversion into photons. In
demonstration experiments, we can simulate axion signals by introducing
oscillating magnetic fields aligned with the protosolenoid, providing an
opportunity to test and refine the BabyIAXO design for actual axion research.

The occupation number over time is analyzed for a bosonic oscillator coupled to a reservoir with self-interaction. This oscillator has tunable properties and the research yields two types of stationary solutions: one where energy levels remain constant and another type that exhibits periodic oscillations. Within the class of bosonic oscillators, there is a non-zero stiffness that allows for self-oscillating behavior even without an external thermal reservoir.

We introduce DexGraspNet, a massive synthetic dataset designed for robotic
grasp planning, featuring over 1.5 million diverse grasp configurations for
approximately 10,000 commonly encountered objects commonly found in everyday
life. Unlike existing datasets, our Grasp-Net is pre-generated through
simulation, eliminating the need for physical object manipulation. Each object
is simulated using a physics engine and rendered through a camera, with synthetic
grasp trajectories obtained via Monte Carlo Tree Search. Notably, our object set
is constructed from real-world CAD data, and we utilize a combination of
synthetic and actual images to bridge the reality gap. To assess the effectiveness
of our dataset, we trained a large number of successful grasp policies for
various robotic arms. Through extensive real-world trials involving 10,000
grasp attempts, our proposed dataset has demonstrated exceptional versatility and
adaptability. Furthermore, our proposed dataset is now available for public
access at https://dexgraspnet.github.io.

A novel motion compensation technique is introduced to enhance free-breathing four-dimensional MRI imaging. This approach utilizes real-time MRI feedback to track and track the motion of the scanner table, allowing it to adjust image reconstruction in response to movement. A compressed sensing method is used to produce high-quality images from the adjusted data, demonstrating the efficacy of this approach in the abdominal and chest regions. Furthermore, an optimized acquisition strategy is developed to balance image quality and scan duration, achieving successful results in retaking data in response to movement and producing artifact-free images. Successful results are demonstrated in the chest and abdominal regions, where high-quality images are obtained in approximately 15 minutes.

Model compression through knowledge distillation has become a widely used method,
yet previous research has not thoroughly examined how the knowledge from large,
complex models can be transferred to their smaller counterparts. This study
investigates the knowledge transfer process through information flow and develops
a new method called InDistill, which leverages an intermediate layer to preserve
key relationships and dependencies within the large model. By applying InDistill
to both linear and non-linear small models, the technique enhances the ability to
transfer learned information and significantly improves the accuracy of model
compression. In particular, InDistill achieves notable gains of up to 1.5% in
next-token prediction tasks and 9.5% in classification tasks.

Topological equivalence of submersion functions implies topological equivalence to a submersion function in two-dimensional linear-like scenarios. The linear-like case involves conditions where the linear component A of the function f satisfies a certain rank requirement. The proof relies on the Planar Thom-Mather Theorem and demonstrates that the rank of the Jacobian of h at the origin exceeds zero due to the submersion properties of f.

Ecosystems' dynamics are heavily influenced by human consumption of biomass, a factor that varies across space and time. Human-driven resource extraction, or non-local grazing, occurs when livestock are moved to new areas for feeding purposes. This study uses a stochastic model, incorporating an existing deterministic framework, to simulate vegetation dynamics in response to non-local grazing. By considering both space and time variability in non-local grazing, the research explores the effects of this practice on vegetation dynamics, particularly focusing on the mean vegetation cover and its variability. By analyzing the moments of the vegetation distribution, the results indicate that increased non-local grazing intensity leads to a decrease in ecosystem stability and the likelihood of reaching a critical threshold, potentially triggering a sudden transition to a desert state.

A well-known dimensionality reduction technique, CountSketch, is frequently used in both online and offline algorithms to rapidly approximate the core property of vectors. However, when dealing with adaptive inputs that include carefully crafted queries, these techniques can fail. In an effort to address this limitation, a research study has established a significant finding: for any CountSketch-based algorithm with only a constant degree of freedom, there exists an adaptive input sequence that will cause the estimated values to deviate significantly from their true counterparts, exceeding the highest norm by a factor of at least $n^{\Omega(d)}$. This discovery also leads to the conclusion that online CountSketch is incapable of achieving sublinear multiplicative error in worst-case scenarios, a limitation that holds true for significant metrics such as the $\ell_p$ norms. In response to this challenge, a counterexample is also presented which demonstrates the impossibility of achieving accurate estimates for general CountSketch with any choice of parameters.

We have created the ipie package, which is an auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo program with flexible and efficient capabilities on both CPUs and GPUs through a hybrid C++/Python architecture. This package combines a finely optimized C++ engine for high-performance calculations and a user-friendly Python interface for ease of use. Detailed documentation and comprehensive tutorials are included to facilitate the adoption of this tool, which is available for download at ipie.readthedocs.io. Our approach includes the development of a C++ engine incorporating advanced Monte Carlo algorithms, such as the fixed-node auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo and the multilevel multireference diffusion Monte Carlo methods, as well as stochastic reconfiguration. By incorporating a tensor contraction optimization library and a GPU-accelerated linear algebra package, we have achieved a high level of efficiency in our simulations. Our work also includes the development of a user-friendly Python interface, which enables a wide range of auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo methods and linear algebra packages to be utilized in a seamless manner.

High-frequency trading, a rapid-fire method of buying and selling stocks, relies heavily on advanced algorithms to take advantage of fleeting market opportunities. By harnessing the potential of quantum computing, we've designed a modified version of the quantum Prisoner's Dilemma game, simulating a scenario where two players, utilizing both local and entangled bases, can achieve a cooperative outcome even without prior communication. Local entanglement is demonstrated to be as effective as global communication in the traditional game setup. The significance of this game theory model is then examined in the context of high-frequency trading, where the proposed model is tested using the IBM quantum computer.

A seller is selling an indivisible item to a group of customers who make offers to the seller directly or through intermediaries. The goal is to create a strategy that maximizes revenue by taking into account the customers' offers. The setting assumes that the intermediaries act in the seller's best interest and the customers' valuations can be described by random variables. The random variables are described by specific families of distributions where the parameters are known and the seller knows the class of distributions but not the parameters. The goal is to create a strategy that maximizes revenue by taking into account the sales process. The analysis shows that the seller can achieve revenue close to what is possible when the seller knows the customers' valuations. To facilitate abstractive summarization, we've developed an automatic planning
method based on an encoder-decoder structure. We've utilized knowledge graph entities
as planning units and employed trained entity prompts, which have shown effectiveness in
few-shot classification tasks, within the attention mechanism to efficiently identify
relevant graph entities and reduce summarization distractions. Experimental results
on the XSum dataset demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms the baseline,
and highlight the capability of generating an entity-based plan as a useful tool for
enhancing the interpretability of generated summaries.

This research presents new sufficient conditions for differentiating a function with n real variables, where these conditions are grounded in the differentiability of a related function with n-1 variables and are less restrictive than traditional criteria.

Human vocal synchronization in conversations is a key social connection that also mirrors brain interconnectivity.  Current automated methods for tracking this synchronization in conversations are inefficient and require extensive manual adjustments.  To address this inefficiency, we developed a technique that adapts to different contexts within conversations, demonstrating its effectiveness with a diverse set of conversations.  Compared to standard approaches, our method demonstrated synchronization estimates that were both accurate and consistent across various contexts, thus requiring less manual adjustments.

A lambda-calculus extension, called Lambda-S1, incorporates a control operator that allows non-local control flow, akin to the yield operator, within a strictly sequential quantum computational framework. This formal system is grounded in basic sequential quantum lambda calculus. Concurrently, a categorical model based on Comonadic-Qubit has been developed to ensure the denotational correctness of Lambda-S1. Furthermore, through the application of a pushout construction, it has been demonstrated that certain well-known functional programming techniques can be effectively integrated into Lambda-S1.

Analytical calculations have been performed for two types of two-quasiparticle form factors: the chirality and the overlap with the reduced two-quasiparticle wave function, in relation to wave functions composed of Slater determinants. Wave functions that incorporate a Jastrow factor, which is the leading term in the quasiparticle series expansion, have also been studied. It has been observed that quasiparticle formation is a gradual process, which is more pronounced in lower Landau levels and at higher values of nu. Furthermore, the study found that form factor magnitudes are larger for configurations where the two quasiparticles are in close proximity, and that these magnitudes are more pronounced in lower Landau levels. It has been found that quasiparticle formation is more pronounced in the edge state, which is the state with the highest angular momentum.

To solve the Stokes type variational inequality, which is used in glaciology, a second-order finite element method is applied along with the Lagrange multipliers. This type of inequality has been previously analyzed by Bonnet and Garrahan, leading to an optimal error estimate in terms of the mesh size h for its solution u and the corresponding pressure p, as established in Theorem 1.1. This theorems relies on specific assumptions regarding the domain $\Omega$, boundary $\partial \Omega$, and Lagrange multiplier $\lambda$. This theorems further demonstrates that if these assumptions are met, including approximating the Lagrange multiplier $\lambda$ with finite elements, the error estimates for u and p can be optimized.

We utilized the Science Operations and Outflows with Velocity and Temperature Excitation with a Grid-based Telescope (DUVET) to study how massive star formation affects the evolution of a nearby starburst galaxy. By combining DUVET's high-resolution maps of the 12CO J=1-0 emission with XMM-Newton's spectroscopy, we found that the X-ray emission from the galaxy drives a large-scale outflow of the interstellar medium. The strength of the outflow is directly related to the rate of massive star formation, and this outflow is predicted to be responsible for the observed reduction in the cosmic star formation rate at a redshift of 2.

Our analysis examines the evolution of anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, incorporating detailed nuclear geometry and partonic-quarky phase transitions. We specifically investigate the multiphase transport model's capacity to replicate the $v_3$ triangular flow observed in Au+Au and Cu+Au collisions at a laboratory energy of 200 GeV. The findings indicate that the multiphase transport model aligns well with the experimental measurements for $v_3$ in Au+Au collisions, while also providing insights into the influence of geometric effects on the initial state and evolution of elliptical and triangular energy density distortions.

Our proposed approach, SyncRoB, is a unified platform that facilitates the
development of studies on the coordination of robotic systems across multiple
robtics research domains. This innovative framework is built on a modular
architecture, allowing for the integration of multiple robotic models and
simulators, and is supplemented by a versatile set of robotic components and
tools. This paper presents the design and implementation of SyncRoB, along with
a description of its existing robotic components and tools, and showcases its
application and adaptability to various robotic systems. Furthermore, the paper
introduves the synchronization middleware, which provides a standardized
interface for implementing coordination algorithms and exchanging data
between robotic systems, as well as the simulation subsystem, which enables
algorithm testing and evaluation using synchronous robotic simulations. The
paper also highlights the synchronization tools, which offer a standardized
interface for implementing coordination algorithms and data exchange between
robotic systems, as well as the visualization and monitoring tools. Finally, the
paper demonstrates the practical applicability of SyncRoB and its toolset
through the development of a simulation-based experiment on coordinated robotic
systems and robot path planning.

Deep neural network training for semantic segmentation requires significant computational resources and expert labeling, making transfer learning from pre-trained models a more feasible option. A new approach utilizes a monocular depth estimation model as a starting point, where the depth prediction network's weights are then adapted for semantic segmentation. Surprisingly, the selected depth model outperforms our proposed method, which combines depth and semantic segmentation tasks, even with limited data. Surprisingly, the selected depth model also surpasses the current state-of-the-art model in semantic segmentation, especially when using a complex, multi-layer network for feature extraction.

This study aims to enhance the bounds of the Bohr radius for the group of starlike log-harmonic mappings, denoted by $\mathcal{LS}(r, \theta)$ for $0 \leq r < \pi/2$. We demonstrate that for all such mappings within the unit disk $\mathbb{D}$, the following Bohr radius bound applies: $r_B(G_{S_L}) = r_B(\mathcal{LS}(r, \theta)) = \min\{1, \sqrt[3]{\frac{1-r\cos\theta}{1+r\cos\theta}e^{2}}\}$. Our results are substantiated using both numerical and analytical methods.

A nonparametric measure of correlation known as Kendall's tau is examined, with an emphasis on an efficient estimation method for large datasets. The existing efficient estimator involves intricate calculations, leading to a simplified, yet competitive alternative, the asymptotically optimal jackknife-ARN estimator. This new approach is supported by simulation results that show it performs similarly to the more advanced estimator when it comes to making predictions.

The integration of edge computing and vehicular networks within the Internet of Things has given rise to edge intelligence, a concept that enables fog nodes to assist vehicles in achieving their objectives. However, concerns regarding data security and confidentiality persist when vehicles share their information with these fog nodes. This research presents a comprehensive framework for safeguarding vehicle data when it is collected from the fog node. A joint learning approach is proposed, combining federated learning and proxy reencryption, to enable the fog node to process and return processed data to the requesting vehicle while preserving its confidentiality. This proposed system was implemented using the PyFedRL library, which combines PyTorch and a secure multi-party computation library, along with a custom traffic simulation tool. Experimental results indicate that the proposed framework offers an effective means of securing vehicle data, while also demonstrating that proxy reencryption has a negligible impact on the overall data training process.

This study introduces a novel class of surfaces, referred to as Euler Characteristic surfaces, and investigates their fundamental properties. We demonstrate that for a surface S of this class, the mean curvature is directly proportional to its Gaussian curvature. We identify a normal vector field that is preserved under these surfaces and show they are inherently constant mean curvature surfaces. We also establish a relationship between their associated family and the Catenoid-Roman Surface. Additionally, it is proven that for a closed Euler Characteristic surface of genus g, the volume it encloses can be maximized only if it is a sphere.

This study explores a predation interaction between two species, applying a specific loss term to the prey population that adheres to Strong Allee conditions, and considers the effects of in-diffusion on spatial models with no-penetration boundaries. We derive precise formulas for spatial coexistence and spatial coexistence with zero predator populations. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that spatial models exhibit various long-term behaviors, including stable coexistence, periodic solutions, and patterns of half- and full-separation, along with certain bifurcations.

This study builds on a series of findings regarding the facet pivot method for solving linear programming problems by providing an even tighter iteration limit. Initially developed in 2009, the facet pivot method offers an adaptive approach to traversing the simplex algorithm, which has been proven to take no more than O(n) steps. In this part II of a two-part series, an even tighter bound of O(n) is established, which linearly depends on the rank of the cost matrix. Specifically, for 2-dimensional projection matrices, the number of iterations is limited to five times the rank, and for matrix dimensions of n, a similar but slightly looser bound of seven times the rank is established. In addition, for problems where the cost matrix rank is even, the number of iterations is limited to four times the rank plus three, and for odd ranks, the number of iterations is limited to four times the rank plus one, and these bounds are considered tight.

We explore the NK1 group of Bak's unitary group U over a ring R with an automorphism σ equal to its inverse, which is equipped with a Hermitian form. We also look into how the K1 group of R affects its quotient ring R/(2R), particularly in relation to U and a related quotient group. Our analysis is based on a graded ring's properties, specifically that it has a square in a particular ideal and that its Nakayama functor is an equivalence. Under these conditions, we establish an isomorphism between the K1 group of R and its quotient ring R, which has significant implications for understanding the K1 group of R.

This paper undertakes a thorough comparison of the comprehensive, off-shell 
WW production cross-section and total W boson production rates, both in single and 
pair forms, to understand their influence on the precision with which the W and top 
quark masses can be determined using the invariant mass of the quark produced in ttj events. 
Our findings suggest that neglecting off-shell effects can result in a substantial 
bias in the extracted top quark mass, amounting to as much as 0.5 GeV. 
Additionally, we propose a novel method for measuring the W production rate 
in the channel gg -> Wg, which is typically disregarded in analyses focused on 
ttj events.

Recent advancements in deep learning have made vision-based anti-spooing models highly effective, but these models often require substantial, annotated data and struggle with diverse attack methods. Self-supervised learning techniques have shown promise in reducing the reliance on labeled data, yet these methods can be challenging to apply due to their complex training processes. In this research, we explore the use of pre-trained Vision Transformer (ViT) models for self-supervised learning and zero-shot evaluation in the context of 3D face spoofing, utilizing the MegaFace database. Our findings indicate that using pre-trained ViT models can yield superior performance compared to conventional methods, achieving substantial improvements in spoof detection accuracy, particularly for challenging attack types.

Deep reinforcement learning has emerged as a promising technique for autonomous driving. A novel application of this method is proposed, which formulates the autonomous driving problem as a multi-agent task. The proposed method involves a comprehensive simulation environment that simulates various driving scenarios, including diverse road layouts and vehicle dynamics. By treating the map and other vehicles as dynamic inputs, a driving policy is developed to generate steering wheel commands. The proposed method also employs a complex reward function to address multiple driving challenges. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach.

A parallel variant of the NSGA-II algorithm was enhanced through the introduction of a refined parent selection method, aimed at minimizing the influence of evaluation order and the subsequent evaluation time disparities among solutions. The novel approach, termed frequency-based tournament selection, was incorporated into the NSGA-II framework to create PB-PEMOGA, a parallel evolutionary algorithm. By integrating this method, PB-EMOGA successfully mitigates evaluation time bias and accelerates convergence toward the Pareto front, outperforming existing parallel variants such as pNSGA-II and showing greater robustness in handling various problem complexities.

The initial detection of a microlensing event, OGLE-2017-BLG-1434, revealed a binary system that includes a low-mass planet orbiting a star classified as a late M dwarf. This finding was based on the microlensing light curve's extended caustic structure, which allowed researchers to pinpoint the binary nature of the lens. A detailed analysis, incorporating high-resolution data from the Hubble Space Telescope and Keck/NIRC2, further constrained the lens parameters. A comprehensive model, combining ground-based and space-based data, identified the system as hosting a 2.6 M⊕ planet at a distance of 1.2 au from its host star. This planet, with an estimated mass of 2.6±0.3 M⊕, has a low equilibrium temperature of 190±10 K, making it the first known super-Earth planet to directly confirm its orbital parameters through microlensing observations.

The high-frequency expansions of time-periodic Lindblad generators have been
developed to derive explicit expressions for the steady states of driven open quantum
systems at high driving strengths. In this work, we expand upon previous work by Mielke
et al. to provide a more detailed analysis, including an investigation into how rapidly
the expansion converges. Additionally, we analyze the convergence rate of the Trakhtenbrot
algorithm, which is used to calculate the expansion, and demonstrate its application
through studies of specific experimental systems.

Our study of the rare-earth transition metal compounds CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ with
various compositions, focusing on CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ where $x$ equals 0.05,
0.15, 0.25, 0.35, and 0.4, has been conducted using a range of neutron scattering
methods. These include diffraction, small-angle scattering, and inelastic scattering.
These experiments were used to analyze the structural and magnetic properties of the
compounds. Neutron diffraction revealed that the compounds crystallize in the
hexagonal P6/mmm space group with no superstructure or rhombohedral distortion.
However, small-angle neutron scattering detected the presence of large grains.
This was further supported by the observation of a sharp depolarization of the neutron
beam in the time-of-flight spectra. This behavior was found to be dependent on both
the sample and the wavelength.
These findings suggest that the depolarization is due to the ferromagnetic domains
within the sample.
Inelastic neutron scattering revealed a significant increase in the magnetic moment
of Ce in CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ with increasing rhodium concentration up to
x=0.25, after which it decreased.
This was accompanied by a significant broadening of the magnetic excitations.
These results are interpreted as being due to

A newly identified high-mass star-forming region, designated G176.51+00.20, has been discovered using 15-millimeter Very Large Array observations. The data indicates a compact continuum source, and further studies using ALMA have revealed a massive protostar with a surrounding envelope. Narrow-line self-absorbed (nls) HI features in the region's vicinity are also detected, and their properties are analyzed. The temperature of the background continuum source is determined to be 10.8 kelvin, and the HI features exhibit a range of temperatures, velocities, and column densities. The HI features' temperatures are found to be significantly lower than the background temperature, and their column densities are comparable to those in the region's vicinity. The HI features' magnetic field strengths are also calculated, and their origin is discussed in relation to the star-forming region's evolution.

We demonstrate a connection between two types of ergodic transformations, which may seem unrelated at first glance. Both β-shifts and their variations, where a specific interval is excluded or "holed," exhibit ergodic properties. By showing that any β-shift transformation can be transformed into a β-shift with a hole through a specific, measure-preserving isomorphism, we reveal a deeper relationship. This result also allows us to calculate the entropy of such transformations, which is determined by the size of the excluded interval, or "hole."

Determining the CP-violating phase phi_s in Bs to J/psi pi plus pi minus decays was carried out using a dataset of 8,317 phi_s measurements, with a 7,300 fb^-1 integrated luminosity. A novel technique, utilizing matrix element weighting, was developed to mitigate detector biases. The resulting phi_s value of 0.02 ± 0.16 (statistical) ± 0.08 (systematic) rad. aligns with the Standard Model prediction.

Deep Neural Networks have demonstrated remarkable proficiency in handling vast datasets.
Their core principle involves learning intricate patterns from data, with these patterns being utilized for inferences.
However, the effectiveness of these models is contingent upon the similarity between training and testing data.
This study investigates the efficacy of Domain Adaptation techniques in enhancing the performance of DNNs.
By applying these methods to a deep convolutional neural network trained on the ImageNet dataset, we analyze their impact.
This analysis is performed using a GPU, with results indicating that a single NVIDIA V100 can process a batch in 1.5 seconds.
Our findings reveal significant improvements in classification accuracy and efficiency upon incorporating Domain Adaptation techniques.

In this study, we determine a precise estimate for the number of specific types of arcs within the finite field F_q^2, particularly those with specific curvature and gradient properties near 0. Our findings have significant implications in various aspects, such as local cyclotomic sums and arc-specific Fourier analysis.

A pictorial proof demonstrates that exactly $\frac{n^2(n+1)^2}{16}$ distinct equilateral triangles can be found within the $n \times n \times n$ triangular grid, by dividing the total number of triangles into four categorized groups based on the lengths of their sides, which are $n+1$, $n$, $n-r$, or $n-2r$ respectively.

Recent advances in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown great potential in addressing complex problems involving graph-structured data. However, GNNs face significant challenges in providing explanations for their predictions, which is essential for building trust in their applications. Current methods for offering explanations in deep learning models are often tailored to specific GNN architectures and prediction tasks. In this research, we present a versatile model explanation method that can be applied to various GNN models and different prediction tasks in both node classification and graph classification scenarios. Our proposed method uses a parametric approach, where we train a model to assess the importance of specific graph nodes and their features by utilizing variations in predictions from original and perturbed graphs. Our method stands out for its ability to adapt to different GNN models and graph classification settings without requiring any modifications, offering an explicit explanation of its node importance. Our findings demonstrate the effectiveness of our method across various graph classification settings.

The peculiar cluster, RXCJ0232.2-4420, is located at a distance of 2.3 billion light years and features an unusual central void and two bright substructures. An analysis of X-ray data from the XMM-Newton space telescope has allowed researchers to study the shape of the gas in this cluster and the energy exchanges between galaxies and the surrounding gas. A study of the X-ray surface brightness has shown that the gas in this cluster is not uniform, but rather elongated in the direction of the gas streams. A study of the gas temperatures in this cluster has revealed that the gas in these streams is much hotter than the surrounding gas, indicating that the gas in these streams originated from the surrounding galaxies. A study of the gas in this cluster has also revealed that the gas in these streams contains a high level of heavy elements, which is consistent with the presence of a large number of stars in the surrounding galaxies. A study of the gas in this cluster has also revealed that the gas in these streams contains a high level of kinetic energy, which is consistent with the presence of a large number of galaxies in the surrounding region.

Recently, the Legendre Memory Unit (LMU), a type of recurrent neural network,
has been developed and is capable of solving complex tasks such as
sequence-to-sequence prediction. Its training process, however, is hindered by
a non-differentiable mechanism, which causes the loss gradient to be zero and
prevents the model from being trained in parallel. This issue is resolved by
introducing the dual network, which is used to estimate the loss gradient and
enable the model to be trained in parallel. This approach is then applied to
train the dual network and a concatenated network, which is used to update the
model parameters in parallel. The performance of the model is evaluated on
various benchmark datasets and a range of prediction tasks, and the results
show that the model can be trained in parallel without compromising its
performance.

A wide variety of sub-GeV particles, beyond neutrinos, may interact weakly and potentially form dark matter. We introduce an array of cutting-edge experiments and techniques aimed at detecting such particles, many of which represent the forefront of dark matter research. By combining theoretical frameworks with experimental approaches, we illustrate how these studies can not only identify dark matter but also probe the parameter spaces predicted by theories like neutrinoless double beta decay, quantum gravity, and sterile neutrinos.

The development of human language is characterized by the creation of new words, modifications to existing words, and the eventual disappearance of words that are no longer used. This process is complicated by the challenge of reaching a stable and universally understood vocabulary. In an effort to understand how a shared vocabulary can be achieved, we examine the dynamics of word migration between mobile individuals through the use of a modified naming game that simulates the exchange of words between agents. This modified game reveals that a stable vocabulary emerges as a result of a phase transition, facilitated by the agents' movement and migration. This outcome provides a theoretical framework for explaining the natural process of language evolution and development.

PINN algorithms have been developed to solve partial differential equations, but they struggle with equations that have complex solutions, especially when the data is sparse. To address this issue, researchers have proposed adding a momentum term to the gradient update in the backpropagation process. Our study investigates the impact of using momentum in PINN and the role of spectral bias on its effectiveness. By introducing a spectral bias in the network structure, earlier studies have shown that it can accelerate training. However, our results indicate that using momentum can counteract the benefits of spectral bias. To address this issue, a modified version of the spectral bias is proposed, which is shown to improve the convergence of the algorithm.

We consider a system of two waves over a bounded domain in n dimensions (where n equals 3 or 4), where one wave has Kelvin-Voigt damping over the entire domain and the other wave has damping that is confined to a subregion which may be very small, provided it's not too tiny, and this partial damping has a viscoelastic property. A unique global solution exists for this system when waves are coupled by a power function with an exponent greater than or equal to 4 in the 3D case and greater than 3 in the 4D case. By using multipliers techniques, we establish the asymptotic stability of the solution, where it decays polynomially over time.

In recent years, deep reinforcement learning has demonstrated remarkable success.
Nevertheless, the complexity of its models makes the learning process a "black box,"
which hinders the development of trust and the incorporation of domain knowledge.
In this research, a method combining logical knowledge and hierarchical learning is
proposed to facilitate the incorporation of domain expertise.
The proposed approach, called IMH-Learning, integrates inductive logic programming
to create a hierarchical model.
By doing so, it enables the development of more efficient hierarchical policies.
We tested IMH-Learning's effectiveness using two sets of experiments based on PyBullet
environments, which yielded improved sample efficiency and policy performance.

Conventional optical nonreciprocity is typically achieved by utilizing magnetic fields or similar mechanisms to break symmetry. This work explores an approach for generating wide-band optical nonreciprocity through the interaction of a quantum field with a parametrically driven two-level system. This mechanism circumvents the necessity of breaking spatial symmetry. Our proposed quantum nonreciprocity is examined through an examination of the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation, and its potential implementation is analyzed by investigating the flow of spin angular momentum within the quantum medium. Our theoretical findings indicate that quantum nonreciprocity exhibits greater efficiency compared to magnetic methods, thereby expanding the range of quantum nonreciprocity applications.
We provide solutions to the general Fenton type minimax optimization problems that involve the sum of functions with translated components, and we provide a specific example of its practical use.

The CRESST experiment, which is one of the most sensitive dark matter detectors using $^6$Li-garnet, is expected to detect signals from $^6$Li nucleon-spin interactions with particles weighing between 0.1 GeV and 10 GeV at the 90% confidence level in 200 days of data collection. This study demonstrates that the experiment will be able to detect signals from spin-dependent interactions with cross-sections up to $10^{-41}$ cm$^2$, particularly when targeting the region of the parameter space that has not been constrained by other experiments.

Blind Image deblurring attempts to reverse the effects of a kernel without
knowing the kernel's exact form in advance. This research contributes
